title: Heralded high-dimensional module-based quantum computation
authors: Xiao Zhang, Wen-Qiang Liu, Hai-Rui Wei
abstract: Parity measurements have been explored as building blocks for preparing and discriminating entangled states, as well as for implementing quantum computation. We first develop two alternative high-dimensional generalized parity modules, and then propose a procedure for constructing high-dimensional generalized module-based controlled-NOT gate. The construction of module-based quantum computing introduced here is deterministic, heralded, insensitive to the dimensionality of the computing basis, and postselection technique is not required. The result shows that out of $(d-1)!$ generalized parity modules, only modules $ \mathcal{P}=(j\ominus i)\bmod d$ and $ \mathcal{P}=(j \oplus i)\bmod d$ can be used as building blocks for high-dimensional quantum computing. Furthermore, we proposed an optical nondestructive scheme for implementing generalized parity module through quantum nondemolition measurements, and the success of the parity module is heralded by photon-number-resolving detectors and single-photon detectors.
summary: The paper presents a method to build high-dimensional controlled-NOT (CNOT) quantum gates using generalized parity modules. The construction is heralded and deterministic, overcoming limitations of previous schemes by identifying only two usable module types. This work advances the feasibility of qudit-based quantum computation in optical systems.
main_problem: The goal is to develop deterministic, heralded, and dimensionality-insensitive methods for constructing high-dimensional module-based quantum computation gates.
main_result: The authors successfully constructed a generalized controlled-NOT (CNOT) gate using only two specific types of parity modules out of all possible possibilities. This scheme requires no postselection and generalizes to arbitrary qudit dimensions ($d$).
method: They propose constructing the CNOT gate via sequential operations involving generalized parity modules, Fourier transformations, and ancillary qubits/qudits.
model_or_system: The system involves high-dimensional quantum states (qudits) where computation is built upon 'generalized parity modules,' which are implemented optically using Orbital Angular Momentum (OAM) degrees of freedom in single-photon systems.
key_observables: The success of the parity module operation is heralded by specific detection outcomes from photon-number-resolving and single-photon detectors.
important_parameters: The dimensionality $d$ of the qudit basis, and the structure of the two usable parity modules: $\mathcal{P}=(j\ominus i) mod d$ and $\mathcal{P}=(j \oplus i) mod d$.
main_assumptions: The scheme assumes the ability to implement quantum nondemolition measurements for the parity module and relies on specific detection events (e.g., no firing of certain detectors) to confirm gate success.
figures_summary: Figures schematically illustrate the construction of the generalized CNOT gate using blocks like $P_1$, $P_2$, and Fourier transformations ($F_d$), showing the optical components involved in parity sorting.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the concept and constructs the CNOT gate for qutrits, then generalizes this construction mathematically to arbitrary qudit dimensions ($d \ge 4$) using linear algebra and state evolution equations. Finally, it details an optical implementation scheme utilizing OAM encoding.
why_interesting: This work provides a robust theoretical framework for building universal quantum gates in high-dimensional Hilbert spaces using measurement-based techniques, which is crucial for scaling up photonic quantum computation beyond simple qubit systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The schematic diagram for constructing a deterministic high-dimensional generalized CNOT gate. Blocks P1 and P2 are two generalized parity modules. Fd denotes the qudit-based Fourier transformation, which performs the transformation |m⟩→ 1 √

Figure 2: Schematic diagram of generalized qutrit-based parity module. D and D denote photon-number-resolving detector and single-photon detector, respectively. F3 is qutrit-based Fourier transformation. The circuits in the dashed boxes are designed to measure the output photon in the basis {|0⟩, |1⟩, |2⟩}.

Figure 3: Schematic diagram of a first-order parity sorter (PS1) [49]. Dove prism flips the transverse cross section of the beam in one arm while leaving the other unchanged. This Mach-Zehnder interferometer routes the photons with even ℓ(l mod 2 = 0) to Port B1 (transmitted) and those with odd ℓ(l mod 2 = 1) to Port A1 (reflected).

Figure 4: Schematic diagram of a second-order parity sorter (PS2) [51]. This interferometric device classifies OAM modes by ℓmod 4. The device transmits photons with ℓmod 4 = 0 (e.g., |0⟩, | ± 4⟩), and reflects the photons with l mod 4 = 2 (e.g., | ± 2⟩, | ± 6⟩). For the photons with odd ℓ(e.g., | ± 1⟩, | ± 3⟩), they are randomly led to the two output ports.
